title: A New Flying Drone Uses Touch to Perch Like a Bird
summary:
A new flying robot can feel its way onto a branch and hang there, just like a bird settling in for a rest. Its three human-inspired fingers grasp many shapes, letting the robot "hang out" in one spot.

Perching could let drones stay in one place for long periods, monitoring factories and power lines -- or exploring remote places. But roboticists have found it hard to help drones get a grip.

Many drones rely on vision to perch, but in crowded spaces vision can be blocked and the robot may fail to attach. Sometimes even its own grippers block its view. The new design relies on touch sensors instead. Once attached, its three fingers hold on with no extra energy. Researchers described the design August 22 in npj Robotics.

Anton Bredenbeck, a roboticist at Delft University of Technology, wanted a robot to study vulnerable ecosystems -- but it would need to stay put. "The problem," Bredenbeck says, "is that drones are really, really inefficient flyers." A drone could not fly nonstop for a month, so his team decided to attach their flyers to the environment instead.

Birds inspired the approach: they use vision to spot a perch from a distance, but touch guides the final moments of landing. The drone grasps things and hangs below, using three fingers positioned like a thumb, pointer finger, and middle finger. Each has three segments of different lengths, known as phalanges, so the grasp adapts to different shapes.

Touch sensors surround silicone pads inside each finger. When they touch something, the drone knows whether to close its fingers. Bendable joints with springs keep the fingers closed, like a clothespin's springs. A motor opens them by pulling metal cords that act like tendons in human fingers. "I was really surprised how well that worked," Bredenbeck says.
why_it_matters: If drones can perch and rest, they could watch over forests, farms, and power lines for weeks without landing to recharge, opening new ways to study nature and keep people safe.

background_read: Drones are flying robots, but they use up energy fast, so they cannot stay in the air for very long.
Perching means landing on something, like a branch, and staying there, which would let a drone rest in one place while it watches an area or explores a remote place.
Birds perch by using sight to find a spot from far away and touch to guide the last moments of landing, and this new drone copies that trick with finger-like grippers and touch sensors.
The drone was built to help study fragile ecosystems, places in nature that are easily harmed and hard for people to reach.
